entries.question: How did Jesus respond when questioned by the high priest?
entries.summary: Matthew 26:64 and Luke 22:70 give Jesus the famously evasive 'thou hast said' / 'ye say that I am' — an answer that can be parsed as a yes, a no, or a 'that's your word, not mine.' Mark 14:62 has him answer with no ambiguity at all: *egō eimi*, 'I am.' Same scene, same question, but Mark's Jesus delivers the unconditional self-identification while Matthew and Luke deflect it back onto the questioner.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization, run by Blomberg and Carson, is that *sy eipas* ('thou hast said') is an idiomatic Semitic affirmation — a yes with deniability built in. Fair enough as background grammar. The problem is that Matthew and Luke clearly know Mark's text and are editing it. Mark's *egō eimi* is the highest-Christology self-declaration in the entire Synoptic tradition, echoing the divine-name formula from Exodus 3:14 and Deutero-Isaiah's 'I am he' sayings. Joel Marcus in the AYB Mark argues Mark intends the reader to catch the theophanic echo — this is the moment Jesus openly claims divine identity, and the Sanhedrin charges him with blasphemy precisely because they hear it that way. Matthew softens that bald *egō eimi* into a circumlocution and adds 'nevertheless I say unto you' to shift the weight onto the Son of Man saying that follows. Luke goes further, splitting the question into two parts (are you the Christ? are you the Son of God?) and giving both a deflective answer. This is exactly the redactional pattern Ehrman documents in *The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture* — where you'd expect later evangelists to *raise* the Christology, here Matthew and Luke are dialing back Mark's direct claim. Why? Probably because the bare *egō eimi* was theologically inconvenient in two directions: it made Jesus' answer sound presumptuous in a way that could embarrass Christian readers, and it made the blasphemy charge stick too cleanly. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, *sy eipas* can affirm. But it doesn't say *egō eimi*. The Greek wording is different and the evangelists chose those wordings deliberately. Take your pick: Mark's unfiltered self-identification or Matthew and Luke's hedge — they're not the same answer.

entries.question: To whom did Peter deny knowing Jesus?
entries.summary: All four gospels agree Peter denied Jesus three times, but they disagree on the cast list. Matthew has a servant girl, then another girl, then a crowd. Mark has a servant girl, then the same girl again, then bystanders. Luke has a servant girl, then a man, then another man. John has a doorkeeper-girl, then anonymous bystanders, then a male servant of the high priest who happens to be the kinsman of the guy Peter sliced an ear off of. Three challengers, three accusations — but the identities don't line up across the four accounts.
entries.commentary: This is one of the densest harmonization problems in the Passion narrative because the 'three denials' tradition is so structurally fixed across all four sources that any divergence in the details has to be explained against a hard count. The standard apologetic move, run by Archer in his *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* and by Blomberg in *The Historical Reliability of the Gospels*, is to argue that Peter actually denied Jesus *more* than three times and each evangelist preserves a different sample of three. That's the John Wenham approach in *Easter Enigma* too. The trouble is that every gospel emphatically says *three* denials and ties the count to the cockcrow prophecy — Mark even has Jesus predict two cockcrows and Peter deny three times before the second one. You can't multiply denials past three without breaking the prophetic framework the evangelists themselves install. The more parsimonious reading from critical scholarship is that Mark established the basic shape (girl, same girl, bystanders) and Matthew, Luke, and John each independently or in chains adjusted the details. Raymond Brown's *Death of the Messiah* lays out the redactional analysis: Matthew swaps Mark's repeat-girl for 'another maid' to avoid the awkwardness of the same person asking twice, Luke replaces the second and third challengers with men because his narrative emphasizes legal-witness framing, and John has the high priest's kinsman because he's already established the ear-cutting detail and wants narrative payoff. Steel-manning the apologist: yes, in a chaotic courtyard with multiple voices, Peter could have been challenged by several people in quick succession and the evangelists could be sampling. But the gospels themselves don't tell that story — each one tells a tidy three-challenge story with specific challengers. Take your pick: either the gospels are each giving a clean account of the same three encounters (and contradicting each other on who) or they're sampling different encounters (and contradicting their own 'three denials' framing).

entries.question: How did Judas die?
entries.summary: Matthew 27:5 has Judas return the silver, throw it down in the temple, and go hang himself — a tidy suicide-by-hanging. Acts 1:18 has Judas buy a field with the blood money, fall headlong in it, and burst open with his bowels gushing out — a graphic falling-apart death with no hanging mentioned. Two New Testament accounts, two completely different mechanisms of death.
entries.commentary: This is the textbook Sunday School contradiction and the apologist responses are equally textbook. The standard harmonization, run by Archer and Geisler and Howe, is to combine the accounts: Judas hanged himself, the rope or branch broke, and his body fell and ruptured. It's mechanically possible — a body left hanging in the Palestinian sun for any length of time would bloat, and a fall onto rocks could split a decomposing corpse open. The trouble is that neither text actually says that. Matthew says Judas hanged himself and stops there. Acts says he fell headlong and burst open, with no mention of a rope. You have to import the missing pieces from one account into the other to make the harmonization run. There's a bigger problem too: the *agent* of the field purchase. In Matthew the chief priests buy the potter's field with the returned silver because they can't put blood money in the treasury. In Acts Judas himself buys the field 'with the reward of iniquity.' That's a separate contradiction (the next entry covers it) but it points to the same diagnosis — these are two independent traditions about the death of Judas circulating in early Christianity, each tied to an etiology for 'the field of blood' (*Hakeldama*), and neither author knows or cares about the other's version. Raymond Brown's *Death of the Messiah* lays out both traditions side by side and concludes they're independent legends developed to explain a known place name in Jerusalem and to satisfy the theological need for Judas to die badly. The Matthean account leans on Old Testament suicide echoes (Ahithophel in 2 Sam 17:23) to make Judas a typological traitor; the Lukan account in Acts leans on graphic divine-judgment death imagery (cf. Antiochus IV in 2 Macc 9:7-12). Two evangelists writing two theological obituaries. Take your pick: harmonize with imported details neither text supplies, or accept that early Christian tradition didn't have one settled story about how Judas died.

entries.question: Who bought the potter's field?
entries.summary: Matthew 27:6-7 has the chief priests buy the potter's field with the silver Judas threw back at them, because as blood money it can't go in the temple treasury. Acts 1:18 has Judas himself buy the field with the same silver. Two New Testament etiologies for the same plot of land — *Hakeldama*, the field of blood — and they can't both be right about who held the deed.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization here, run by Archer and Geisler/Howe, is that Judas 'bought' the field in the indirect sense — *he* provided the money, even if the priests handled the transaction. That kind of indirect-agency reading is sometimes called *qua causa* logic: you did the thing if your money did the thing. The trouble is that Acts 1:18 doesn't read like indirect agency. The Greek is *ektēsato chōrion* — he acquired/bought the field, active voice, Judas as the subject. And the narrative context says he bought it 'with the reward of iniquity,' implying he held the cash and made the purchase. If Luke wanted to say the priests bought the field on his behalf, he had grammatical options to say that and didn't use them. The deeper issue is that the two accounts also disagree on *why* the field is called the field of blood. Matthew says it's because the field was bought with blood money. Acts says it's because Judas's bowels burst out *in* the field — it's blood-stained because of his death there. These are two independent etiological stories preserved in two different communities, each anchoring the field name to a different event. Raymond Brown in *Death of the Messiah* lays this out as a classic case of doublet etiology — both authors knew there was a field called *Hakeldama* near Jerusalem, both connected it to Judas, but each plugged in a different mechanism. Matthew also drags in a tortured prophecy citation ('that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet') which is actually closer to Zechariah 11:12-13 than anything in Jeremiah — itself a known textual problem in Matthew. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, you can read *ektēsato* loosely if you really need to. But neither evangelist tells the harmonized story. They tell two different stories. Take your pick: harmonize by importing missing context that contradicts the active voice of Acts, or accept that early Christian tradition didn't have one settled story about who held the deed to that field.

entries.question: Was Jesus silent during his trial before Pilate?
entries.summary: Matthew 27:12-14 and Mark 15:3-5 have Jesus go silent in front of Pilate — refusing to answer the chief priests, refusing to answer a word, until Pilate himself marvels at how thoroughly Jesus is stonewalling. John 18:33-37 has Jesus and Pilate engage in a full theological back-and-forth about kingship, kingdoms of this world, and bearing witness to the truth. Same trial, same Roman procurator — but in the Synoptics Jesus barely says a word and in John he delivers a small sermon.
entries.commentary: The harmonization apologists reach for, including Carson in his PNTC John, is that the Synoptics and John are reporting different *phases* of the same trial — Jesus answers the initial christological question ('art thou the king of the Jews?') with the short affirmation 'thou sayest it' that all four gospels preserve, then goes silent on the *subsequent* accusations from the priests, which is what the Synoptics emphasize. John, on this reading, expands the initial Pilate-Jesus exchange while the Synoptics compress it. That's a decent reading of the early verses and does soften the contradiction. The trouble is the *character* of the silence in Matthew and Mark. Matthew specifies Jesus 'answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly' — that's the same Markan emphasis on radical wordlessness, deliberately echoing Isaiah 53:7 ('as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth'). Mark is theologically motivated to make Jesus the silent suffering servant. John has the opposite theological program: Jesus is the *Logos*, the speaking word who controls every conversation he's in. In John there is no Gethsemane prayer of anguish, no cry of dereliction from the cross, no silence before Pilate — instead a sovereign Jesus walking through the Passion in command of every exchange. Raymond Brown in *Death of the Messiah* and Bart Ehrman in *How Jesus Became God* both treat this as a deliberate Johannine theological reshaping of the Passion. The Synoptic suffering-servant Jesus and the Johannine sovereign-Logos Jesus are two distinct christological portraits, and the silence-versus-dialogue divergence is one of the cleanest places to see it. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, you can stitch a composite trial in which Jesus speaks at first and then falls silent. But you have to do the stitching — neither Mark nor John presents a composite. Take your pick: harmonized hypothetical or honest acknowledgment of two different Passion theologies.

entries.question: Who put the robe on Jesus?
entries.summary: Luke 23:11 has Herod Antipas and his soldiers dress Jesus in a gorgeous robe during the side-trip to Herod's quarters that only Luke records, before sending him back to Pilate. Matthew 27:27-28, Mark 15:15-17, and John 19:1-2 have Pilate's Roman soldiers strip Jesus and dress him in a purple/scarlet robe inside the praetorium *after* Pilate had already handed him over for scourging. Two different sets of soldiers, two different settings, two different mock-coronations.
entries.commentary: The most common apologist harmonization, run by Wenham in *Easter Enigma* and by Blomberg in *The Historical Reliability of the Gospels*, is that Jesus was dressed in mock royal clothing *twice* — once by Herod's people and once by Pilate's. It's not logically impossible. The trouble is the narrative function of the robe in each gospel. Matthew, Mark, and John all describe a single mock-coronation scene with all the standard elements: stripping, robe, crown of thorns, reed scepter, mock-hailing as king. The robe isn't an incidental wardrobe choice — it's part of the structured ritual humiliation. Luke's Herod-robe scene has none of the other coronation furniture; it's just the robe, and Herod sends Jesus back in it without any of the mock-king ceremony the other three describe. So the harmonization has to posit two robes used for visually similar but narratively distinct mockeries that no single evangelist combines. Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB Luke and Raymond Brown in *Death of the Messiah* both argue the Herod-Antipas trial scene is a Lukan composition — Luke is interested in showing Jesus examined by all the major Palestinian authorities (Sanhedrin, Pilate, Herod) and in fulfilling Acts 4:25-27's reference to Herod and Pilate gathering against the Lord's anointed. The robe shows up in Luke's Herod scene because Luke needs Jesus marked as a 'king' for the dramatic irony, but he relocates the visual mockery away from the Pilate praetorium that Mark established. This is a redactional choice, not an additional historical event. Steel-manning the apologist: yes, two robes is logically possible. But it requires assuming each of the four evangelists has stripped a relevant detail their source provided, and none thought it worth mentioning that Jesus had been mocked with a robe twice. The parsimonious read is that Luke is rewriting where and by whom the mock-coronation happens. Take your pick.

entries.question: What color was Jesus' robe?
entries.summary: Matthew 27:28 says the soldiers put a *scarlet* robe (*chlamyda kokkinēn*) on Jesus. Mark 15:17 and John 19:2 say it was *purple* (*porphyran*). Two different colors named in three different gospels for what is clearly the same mock-coronation robe.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization is that ancient color terminology was fuzzy and 'scarlet' and 'purple' covered overlapping reddish-purple shades, so the difference is a translation artifact rather than a real disagreement. There's something to this — *porphyra* in Greek covered a range from deep red-purple to crimson, and Roman dye technology produced fabrics that read differently in different lights. Tyrian purple, the elite dye, was actually closer to dark red-violet than to modern royal purple. Archer leans on this in his *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties*. The harmonization gets partial credit because the underlying object is plausibly the same garment. But Matthew is *editing Mark*, and his switch from *porphyran* to *chlamyda kokkinēn* — a soldier's red military cloak — is deliberate. Davies and Allison in the ICC argue Matthew is making the garment more realistic: Roman soldiers actually wore red military cloaks (the *paludamentum* / *chlamys*) and dressing Jesus in one fits the mock-king scene better than the expensive Tyrian purple Mark named. Mark wanted royalty symbolism; Matthew wanted historical verisimilitude and went with what soldiers had available. So the contradiction isn't 'they saw different colors' — it's two evangelists making different theological-historical choices about how to dress the mock-king. That's redaction, not memory variation. The Johannine *porphyran* sides with Mark, probably because John is working from a Markan-influenced tradition. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, color terms overlap and ancient red-purple dyes shade into each other. But the Greek words Matthew and Mark use are distinct enough that this still reads as an editorial choice rather than a perception ambiguity. That is of course a judgment call on the redactional intent, but the lexical distinction is real.

entries.question: Who carried Jesus' cross?
entries.summary: John 19:17 has Jesus carry his own cross to Golgotha — explicitly, *bastazōn heautō ton stauron*. Matthew 27:32, Mark 15:21, and Luke 23:26 have Simon the Cyrenian compelled to carry the cross for him. One gospel has Jesus do it himself; the other three have him hand off the load.
entries.commentary: The standard apologist harmonization, run by Carson in his PNTC John and by Blomberg in *Historical Reliability*, is that Jesus started out carrying his own cross from the praetorium and Simon was compelled to take over partway along the route, once Jesus weakened from the scourging. It's a reasonable mechanical reconstruction and it's chronologically possible. The trouble is the *theology* each evangelist is doing with the detail. The Synoptics all have Simon-of-Cyrene because they need somebody else carrying the cross — Jesus is the suffering servant being led like a lamb, exhausted, brutalized, leaning on the path. The Markan Jesus has already fallen silent before Pilate, cried out from the cross 'my God my God why hast thou forsaken me,' and now he can't even carry his own crossbeam. Simon is structurally necessary to the Synoptic Passion. John has the opposite theological program: Jesus is in sovereign command of every event, going to the cross by his own will, and there is no way John lets a third party carry the instrument of his enthronement. John 19:17 is emphatic — Jesus carries it *himself* (*heautō*). Raymond Brown in *Death of the Messiah* and Rudolf Bultmann in his Johannine commentary both treat the omission of Simon as deliberate Johannine theology. The Johannine Jesus does not need help; the Markan Jesus does. Steel-manning the apologist: yes, two-stage cross-carrying is mechanically plausible. But neither John nor the Synoptics tell that two-stage story. John says Jesus carried it; the Synoptics introduce Simon at the start of the Via Dolorosa. Take your pick: redactional theology or the harmonized composite no gospel actually narrates.

entries.question: What did the soldiers give Jesus to drink?
entries.summary: Matthew 27:34 says they offered Jesus vinegar mingled with gall. Mark 15:23 says wine mingled with myrrh. Mark 15:36 and Luke 23:36 later have plain vinegar offered. John 19:29 has vinegar applied with hyssop. Four gospels, at least three different beverage compositions, and arguments to be made about whether some refer to the same offer or separate offers.
entries.commentary: There are actually two separate drink offers in the gospel tradition, which is part of where the harmonization opportunity opens up. The *first* offer is before crucifixion: Mark says wine with myrrh (probably a sedative or mild analgesic, in line with the rabbinic tradition reported in b. Sanhedrin 43a of giving the condemned a stupefying drink). The *second* offer is during the crucifixion: a sour-wine/vinegar (Greek *oxos*) sponge raised to Jesus' mouth, mentioned in all four. So the apologist harmonization, run by Wenham and Blomberg, is that Matthew's 'vinegar and gall' is the same as Mark's 'wine and myrrh' — two ways of describing the same pre-crucifixion sedative — and the later sponge is a separate event. That cleans up a lot of the apparent conflict. But Matthew's specific choice of *cholē* (gall) instead of myrrh is the key. Davies and Allison argue this is Matthew's deliberate edit toward Psalm 69:21 LXX: 'they gave me gall for my meat, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.' Matthew is harmonizing the gospel narrative *to scripture*, not to history — making sure the prophetic text gets cited verbatim. Mark's 'wine and myrrh' is the historically plausible detail (matches the rabbinic anesthetic tradition); Matthew's 'vinegar and gall' is the prophecy-fulfillment redaction. So the contradiction is real but it's not 'what was actually offered' — it's about which evangelist is fitting the event to the psalm. John adds the hyssop detail because hyssop carries Passover symbolism (Exod 12:22) and John has aligned Jesus' crucifixion with the slaughter of the Passover lambs. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, the two-offer reconstruction makes sense and the gall/myrrh swap can be partly explained by Matthew's psalm-targeting. But that swap is itself a redactional choice that distorts the historical detail to match prophecy. That is of course a critical reading, not a face-value reading — but the parsimonious one.

entries.question: What did the sign over Jesus' head say?
entries.summary: All four gospels report the *titulus* nailed to Jesus' cross — but they don't agree on the wording. Matthew 27:37: 'This is Jesus the King of the Jews.' Mark 15:26: 'The King of the Jews.' Luke 23:38: 'This is the King of the Jews.' John 19:19: 'Jesus of Nazareth the King of the Jews.' Four evangelists, four different versions of what was supposedly written on a placard fastened to a cross.
entries.commentary: This is one of the cleanest cases where the harmonization runs into geometry. The apologist response, found in Archer and Geisler/Howe, is that John tells us the sign was written in three languages — Hebrew, Greek, and Latin — and each evangelist may be translating from a different language version, so the variations reflect different translation choices, not a different placard. There's a partial point: trilingual signage was standard Roman practice and the three versions could be expected to differ in word order and detail. But the variations aren't about translation. They're about *content*. Mark has the shortest version (4 words in Greek); Matthew adds 'this is Jesus' (*houtos estin Iēsous*); Luke adds 'this is' but no name; John adds 'of Nazareth.' These are not synonyms in any language — they're additions and subtractions. Raymond Brown in *Death of the Messiah* runs the analysis and concludes the original *titulus* was probably close to Mark's short form ('The King of the Jews' — *ho basileus tōn Ioudaiōn*), and each subsequent evangelist embellished it for their own narrative purposes. Matthew adds the name 'Jesus' so the reader catches the irony that the placard is literally announcing the Christ. Luke smooths the syntax. John adds 'of Nazareth' because his Passion has emphasized Jesus' origin and identity throughout. The Johannine version also functions as set-up for the next verse, where the chief priests ask Pilate to change it from 'The King of the Jews' to 'he said, I am king of the Jews' and Pilate refuses — that argument only works on the longer Johannine titulus. Steel-manning the trilingual harmonization: yes, three languages might produce three different word orders. But it wouldn't produce four different *contents*. The simpler explanation is redactional shaping. Take your pick.

entries.question: Did both thieves revile Jesus?
entries.summary: Mark 15:32 says both of those crucified with Jesus reviled him. Matthew 27:44 says the thieves (plural) cast the same in his teeth. Luke 23:39-43 splits them apart: one malefactor rails on Jesus while the *other* rebukes him, defends Jesus' innocence, and is promised paradise. So Mark and Matthew have both criminals mocking; Luke has one mocking and one converting.
entries.commentary: The standard apologist harmonization, run by Archer, Wenham, and Blomberg, is that *both* criminals initially mocked Jesus (Mark and Matthew capture this early moment) but then *one* of them had a change of heart partway through the crucifixion and became the penitent thief (Luke captures this later moment). It's chronologically possible — crucifixion lasted hours, and someone in agony watching another dying man behave with dignity might plausibly soften his attitude. So the harmonization gets some credit for being mechanically coherent. The trouble is the *function* of the penitent thief in Luke's theology. Luke is the gospel of repentance and the gospel of the marginalized — the good thief is the climactic example of last-minute forgiveness, a structural parallel to the prodigal son and the tax collector. Luke also redacts the cry of dereliction *out* of his crucifixion scene and replaces it with the calm 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.' Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB Luke and Bart Ehrman in *Jesus, Interrupted* both argue Luke is reshaping the entire crucifixion theologically: Mark's anguished, abandoned Jesus becomes Luke's serene, forgiveness-dispensing Jesus, and the penitent thief is part of that reshaping. The thief isn't a historical detail Luke added — he's a theological figure Luke needed. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, the 'one thief changed his mind' reconstruction is internally consistent. And ancient Greek can use plural for generic groups even when only one member acts. But Mark and Matthew don't hint at a conversion, and Luke doesn't hint at an initial mockery from his good thief. Each evangelist tells a complete and self-consistent story. The harmonized story is one no evangelist tells. Take your pick: redactional theology or the imported composite.

entries.question: When was Jesus Crucified?
entries.summary: Mark 15:25 puts the crucifixion explicitly at the third hour — about 9 a.m. Roman reckoning. John 19:14 has Pilate still presenting Jesus to the crowd at the sixth hour — about noon — meaning crucifixion could only begin *after* that. Mark and John can't both be right about when the nails went in.
entries.commentary: This is the most famous chronological contradiction in the Passion narrative, and the harmonization attempts get creative. Augustine in *De Consensu Evangelistarum* III.13 proposed two harmonizations of his own (a *parasceue*-reckoning theory and an attribution of the third-hour clamor to the Jews while the actual nailing-up at the sixth hour was the soldiers' act). The modern apologetic move, articulated by B. F. Westcott in his Gospel of John commentary and picked up by Carson in his PNTC John, is the dual-reckoning hypothesis: John used Roman civil time (counting from midnight) while Mark used Jewish reckoning (counting from sunrise), so John's 'sixth hour' is actually 6 a.m. and Mark's 'third hour' is 9 a.m. — meaning the trial ended at 6 a.m. and the crucifixion happened three hours later, no contradiction. It's an elegant solution. The trouble is that there's no good evidence John uses Roman civil reckoning anywhere else, and significant evidence he uses standard Jewish/Greek daylight-hour reckoning everywhere else (e.g., John 1:39 'tenth hour' clearly means late afternoon, John 4:6 'sixth hour' at the well clearly means noon, John 4:52 'seventh hour' clearly means 1 p.m.). The dual-reckoning theory exists only to solve this one crucifixion-timing problem — which makes it ad hoc by definition. Raymond Brown in *Death of the Messiah* and *Gospel According to John* walks through the proposal and rejects it on consistency grounds. The more parsimonious explanation is that John has theologically relocated the crucifixion. John's Passion is structured around Passover: Jesus is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29), and John times the crucifixion to the slaughter of the Passover lambs in the temple at noon on 14 Nisan, which is exactly when 'the sixth hour' of Passover preparation begins. The Synoptics have Jesus die *on* Passover (after the Last Supper as the Passover meal); John has him die *as* Passover begins, the day before. Bart Ehrman in *Jesus, Interrupted* lays out the chronology problem in detail. The contradiction isn't just hour-of-the-day — it's whether the Last Supper was a Passover meal at all. Steel-manning the apologist: yes, dual-reckoning is theoretically possible. But it's an ad hoc patch applied only here. Take your pick: an unsupported reckoning hypothesis or Johannine paschal theology.

entries.question: What were the last words of Jesus?
entries.summary: Matthew 27:46-50 (following Mark 15:34-37) has Jesus die crying out the cry of dereliction — *Eli Eli lama sabachthani*, 'my God my God why hast thou forsaken me.' Luke 23:46 has him die with a serene self-commendation: 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.' John 19:30 has him die with the triumphant 'It is finished' (*tetelestai*). Three different last words for the same death.
entries.commentary: Even apologists who run the 'all of them, in sequence' harmonization have a hard time with this one because the texts each frame their saying as *the* final cry — the last thing out of his mouth before he yields up the ghost. The harmonization, in Archer and in Wenham's *Easter Enigma*, is to argue Jesus said all three: the cry of dereliction from Mark/Matthew, then 'into thy hands,' then 'it is finished,' then yielded up the spirit, with each evangelist preserving the one they considered most significant. Mechanically possible. Theologically, this is exactly the kind of harmonization that papers over what's actually happening in each gospel. Mark's Jesus dies in anguish and abandonment, quoting Psalm 22 — a deliberately disturbing christological move that Mark uses to emphasize the depth of the suffering and the apocalyptic sense of divine absence. Joel Marcus argues Mark wants the reader to feel the scandal of a crucified messiah who experiences God's withdrawal. Luke read Mark and found that cry intolerable. Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB Luke documents Luke's systematic redaction of the crucifixion scene: cry of dereliction removed, replaced with a calm Psalm 31:5 self-commendation; the women weeping along the way are addressed compassionately; the penitent thief is given paradise; the centurion declares Jesus 'a righteous man' rather than 'the Son of God.' Luke's Jesus dies as a righteous martyr, not an abandoned one. John pushes further still: his Jesus has been in sovereign control of every event of the Passion, and his last word — *tetelestai* — is the completion of a divine plan, not a death-cry but a verdict. Bart Ehrman in *Jesus, Interrupted* lays out the three contrasting Passion theologies with the last-words as the clearest example. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, three sayings in sequence is internally possible. But each gospel writer commits to *its* saying as the climactic one and constructs the whole death scene around it. Take your pick: redactional theology or a composite that erases what each evangelist was actually doing.

entries.question: What did the Centurion call Jesus when he died?
entries.summary: Mark 15:39 and Matthew 27:54 both have the centurion at the cross declare 'Truly this was the Son of God.' Luke 23:47 has the centurion glorify God and say 'Certainly this was a righteous man.' Two different climactic confessions for what is structurally the same Gentile-witness moment.
entries.commentary: This is a small but telling divergence, and it's one of the clearest cases of Lukan redactional theology in the Passion. Mark's centurion is the climactic Gentile witness — the inclusio with Mark 1:1 ('the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God') closes with a Roman soldier finally identifying Jesus by his Markan title. It's the moment the messianic secret breaks. Matthew preserves Mark's wording essentially intact. Luke, working from Mark, changes 'Son of God' to *dikaios* — 'righteous man' or 'just man.' Why? Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB Luke argues this fits Luke's broader portrayal of Jesus as the suffering righteous one in the tradition of Wisdom of Solomon 2-5 and the Maccabean martyrs — Luke's Passion is shaped by the *dikaios paschōn* (suffering righteous man) framework. Throughout Luke 23, Pilate declares Jesus innocent three times, Herod finds no fault, the penitent thief defends his innocence, and now the centurion certifies it. The whole Lukan crucifixion is a forensic vindication scene, and the centurion's *dikaios* is the verdict. Mark/Matthew's *huios theou* serves a different theological program: it's about christological revelation, not legal vindication. The two confessions aren't paraphrases of each other — they're two evangelists making the centurion say what each evangelist's theology requires. Bart Ehrman has noted that Luke's softening of 'Son of God' fits a broader Lukan tendency to dial back high-Christology moments in favor of righteous-martyr framing. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, the centurion could have said both things — there's no rule against multiple comments. Archer goes this route. But each evangelist commits to one declaration as the climactic Gentile testimony. The harmonized 'he said both' story is told by no one. Take your pick.

entries.question: Where did the women watching the crucifixion stand?
entries.summary: Matthew 27:55, Mark 15:40, and Luke 23:49 all describe the women watching the crucifixion *from afar* (*apo makrothen* in the Greek). John 19:25 puts them right next to the cross — Mary the mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene standing close enough that Jesus speaks directly to his mother and the beloved disciple. Three gospels have the women at a distance; one has them at the foot of the cross.
entries.commentary: The standard apologist harmonization, run by Carson in his PNTC John and by Wenham in *Easter Enigma*, is that the women started at the cross (as John reports) and then withdrew to a distance as the crucifixion went on (as the Synoptics describe their position at the moment of death). It's chronologically possible — six hours is long enough to relocate. The problem is that each evangelist freezes the women at a particular position to do specific theological work, and the positions are mutually exclusive at the dramatic moments each evangelist cares about. The Synoptic 'afar off' echoes Psalm 38:11 ('my lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off') — the women are placed at a distance to fit the prophetic image of the righteous sufferer abandoned by those closest to him. Joel Marcus in the AYB Mark catches this allusion. John's close-to-the-cross positioning serves the Beloved Disciple scene of John 19:25-27, where Jesus assigns Mary to the BD's care — that pericope requires the women and the BD to be within earshot. So John needs them near and the Synoptics need them far, for different theological reasons. Raymond Brown in *Death of the Messiah* and *Gospel of John* both note this is a clear case where the Johannine and Synoptic accounts can't be straightforwardly combined — the Beloved Disciple is conspicuously absent from the Synoptic crucifixion entirely, and the Mary-to-BD bequest is unique to John. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, position changes are possible during a multi-hour event. But the harmonized 'they moved closer for the Beloved Disciple scene and then back' is fabricated to reconcile — neither John nor the Synoptics describe any movement. That is of course an inference from redaction, but the parsimonious one.

entries.question: Who buried Jesus?
entries.summary: Matthew, Mark, and Luke all give Joseph of Arimathea sole credit for taking Jesus down, wrapping the body in linen, and laying it in the tomb. John 19:38-42 has Joseph of Arimathea plus Nicodemus burying him together, with Nicodemus supplying a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes. Acts 13:27-29, in Paul's Pisidian Antioch sermon, attributes the burial to 'they that dwell at Jerusalem, and their rulers' — the Jewish authorities, the same people who condemned him. Three different burial parties for the same body.
entries.commentary: The Synoptic-John divergence is mild — adding Nicodemus to the burial party isn't a contradiction so much as a Johannine elaboration, and the standard apologist harmonization simply combines them: Joseph took primary responsibility and Nicodemus assisted. That move works fine because none of the gospels say Joseph acted *alone*; they just don't mention anyone else. The serious contradiction is Acts 13:27-29. Paul (or the Lukan author of Acts speaking as Paul) explicitly attributes the burial to 'they that dwell at Jerusalem, and their rulers' — the same group that 'desired Pilate that he should be slain.' That's the Jewish authorities, not a sympathetic disciple. This is hard to harmonize because it directly contradicts both the Synoptic Joseph-of-Arimathea tradition and the Johannine Joseph-and-Nicodemus tradition, both of which present the burial as an act of devotion by Jesus' supporters. Joseph of Arimathea in Mark is 'an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God' — Matthew and John explicitly call him a disciple. The apologist response, run by Bock in his BECNT Acts commentary and by Witherington in *The Acts of the Apostles*, is to read Acts 13:27-29 as condensed rhetoric — Paul is summarizing that 'the Jews' brought about the death and burial in the loose sense that they triggered the whole sequence of events. Possible but strained: 'they took him down from the tree, and laid him in a sepulchre' is specific enough that 'in the loose sense' isn't a natural read. The critical scholarship — Ehrman in *How Jesus Became God*, John Dominic Crossan in *Who Killed Jesus?* — argues that the historical Jesus likely was buried by his executioners or thrown into a common criminal grave, in line with Roman crucifixion practice, and that the Joseph-of-Arimathea tradition is a later Christian development designed to give Jesus a dignified burial. Acts 13:27-29 may preserve an older, less developed memory of a Jewish-authority disposal of the body. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, 'they' in Acts could be a generalization. But the most parsimonious reading is that the burial traditions developed in different directions in different communities.

entries.question: When did the women (or woman) arrive at the sepulchre?
entries.summary: John 20:1 has Mary Magdalene arrive at the tomb 'early, when it was yet dark' — before sunrise. Matthew 28:1 has the women come 'as it began to dawn.' Mark 16:2 specifies they came 'at the rising of the sun' — explicitly after sunrise. Three sequential moments on the morning timeline, and the gospels can't agree on which one applies.
entries.commentary: On the surface this is the most easily harmonizable contradiction in the resurrection accounts — the difference between 'still dark,' 'dawn,' and 'sunrise' is a window of maybe 30-45 minutes, and you could reasonably argue the women started while it was dark and arrived as the sun rose. Wenham in *Easter Enigma* and Blomberg in *Historical Reliability* both run this version. Fair enough as a rough reconstruction. But the divergence is more interesting when you ask why each evangelist chose the exact wording they did. Mark's *anateilantos tou hēliou* — 'when the sun had risen' — is the most precise solar marker in any of the resurrection accounts, and Mark uses it to anchor the discovery to full daylight, when there's no question of mistaken identity or dim-light error. Matthew softens it to *epiphōskousēi* ('as it began to dawn') because Matthew is more interested in the angelic earthquake and theophanic light than in the time of day. John's *prōi skotias eti ousēs* ('early, while it was still dark') is the deliberate Johannine choice: John has reduced the witnesses to Mary Magdalene alone, and her solo predawn approach fits John's recurring light/darkness motif. She comes in the dark and the resurrection appears in the dawning light. Raymond Brown in *The Gospel of John* commentary treats the Johannine 'still dark' as a theologically loaded detail. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, the timing differences are small and a group of women arriving over a few minutes at different points of pre-dawn could honestly be described all three ways. This is the weakest of the resurrection-narrative contradictions, but it gets sharpened when combined with the other discrepancies (how many women, what they saw, what they did next). On this entry alone, the contradiction is real but minor — harmonization here is more plausible than on most of the surrounding entries. That is of course a judgment call.

entries.question: Who did the women see at the tomb?
entries.summary: Matthew 28:2 has an angel of the Lord descend from heaven, roll back the stone, and sit on it — a single angelic figure. Mark 16:5 has a young man (*neaniskos*) sitting inside the tomb in a long white garment — one figure, not explicitly an angel. Luke 24:4 has two men in shining garments standing by the women. John 20:12 has two angels in white sitting inside the tomb, one at the head and one at the feet of where Jesus had lain. One angel, one young man, two men, two angels — four different tomb-side cast lists.
entries.commentary: The standard apologist harmonization, run by Archer, Wenham, and Geisler/Howe, is the classic 'one doesn't exclude two' move: if Mark and Matthew mention one figure and Luke and John mention two, the gospels that say 'one' simply focused on the speaker while not denying the presence of the other. There's a known principle here — narrators often mention only the figure who matters to their scene, so 'there was an angel' doesn't logically rule out 'there were two angels.' Fair as a logical point. The problem is that Mark and Matthew aren't ambiguous about *focus* — they describe the scene in a way that excludes a second figure. Matthew's angel descends from heaven, rolls the stone, sits on it; he's the only character with a verb. Mark's young man is sitting alone on the right side of the tomb. There's no narrative space being left for a second figure. The bigger contradiction is the *identity*: Mark calls him a *neaniskos*, a young man, without using the word *angelos*. Matthew makes him an angel and adds the descending-from-heaven theophany. Luke pluralizes to two men. John makes them two angels. Joel Marcus and Raymond Brown both treat this as a clear developmental trajectory — Mark's ambiguous young-man figure (which has triggered scholarly debate about whether he's an angelic interpreter or a symbolic disciple) gets explicitly angelified by each subsequent evangelist, and the count escalates from one to two. The doubling is itself a common feature of Lukan and Johannine theophanies (Acts 1:10 also has two men in white at the ascension; the Transfiguration has two figures — Moses and Elijah). Dale Allison's *Resurrecting Jesus* lays out the variations and concludes harmonization fails on cast list. Steel-manning the apologist: yes, partial accounts focusing on the speaker is a real narrative phenomenon. But the cumulative pattern — angel/young-man/two-men/two-angels — looks redactional, not editorial-focus-driven. Take your pick.

entries.question: When did the women discover that Jesus's body was missing?
entries.summary: Luke 24:2-4 and John 20:1-2 have the women (or Mary Magdalene) discover the body is missing *before* they encounter any angelic figure — they enter, find the body gone, and only then do the angels appear (Luke) or Mary runs to tell Peter (John). Matthew 28:5-6 and Mark 16:5-6 have the women see the angel/young man *first*, and only learn from him that the body is gone. Two gospels: discovery, then angel. Two gospels: angel, then announcement.
entries.commentary: The harmonization here gets technical. Apologists like Wenham reconstruct an elaborate sequence: the women approach the tomb at slightly different times, some enter first and discover the empty tomb, then the angel(s) appear, then more women arrive who see the angel before they see inside. This requires the women to split into subgroups arriving at different moments — and it's not what any gospel describes. The simpler reading is that each evangelist has structured the discovery scene to deliver a different theological payload, and the order of events serves that payload. In Mark and Matthew, the women come specifically to anoint the body (Mark 16:1 specifies the spices) and the angelic figure's role is to *correct their assumption* — they expected a corpse, the angel tells them he is risen. The narrative shock requires the angel to deliver the news; the empty tomb is what the angel points to as evidence, not what the women independently verified. In Luke and John, the women (or Mary) discover the emptiness on their own — Luke has them puzzled and perplexed before the angels appear, John has Mary assume body-theft and run to fetch Peter and the Beloved Disciple. Each ordering serves a different theological function: Mark/Matthew use the angel as proclaimer; Luke and John use the women's autonomous discovery to set up subsequent narratives (Peter and BD's run to the tomb in John, the Emmaus road in Luke). Raymond Brown and Dale Allison both treat the four resurrection accounts as drawing on partially independent traditions that each evangelist has shaped, not as multiple eyewitness reports of one event. Steel-manning the apologist: yes, you can construct a sequenced harmonization where some women see the body first and others see the angel first. But it requires inventing a substructure the gospels don't describe and that has the women not telling each other what they just saw. Take your pick.

entries.question: Did the women immediately tell the disciples?
entries.summary: Matthew 28:8 has the women run from the tomb 'with fear and great joy' to bring the disciples word. Luke 24:8-9 has them return from the tomb and tell the eleven and all the rest. Mark 16:8 — the original ending of Mark — has the women flee the tomb, tremble, and 'say nothing to any man, for they were afraid.' Matthew and Luke: immediate proclamation. Mark: shocked silence.
entries.commentary: This contradiction is a famous one because Mark 16:8 is where the earliest manuscripts of Mark stop. The longer endings (Mark 16:9-20) are textually secondary — absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, missing from Eusebius's and Jerome's earliest evidence, and almost universally judged inauthentic by critical text scholars from Westcott-Hort to Metzger to the NA28 editors. So Mark *originally* ends with the women fleeing in silence: *kai oudeni ouden eipan, ephobounto gar*. 'And they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.' That ending was clearly so theologically unsatisfying that the early church manufactured multiple longer endings to fix it. The apologist harmonization, run by Wenham and partially endorsed by Carson, is that Mark means the women said nothing to anyone *on their way* to the disciples — they were silent to bystanders along the road but did eventually deliver the message to the eleven. That's a strained reading of the Greek. Joel Marcus in the AYB Mark and Adela Yarbro Collins in the Hermeneia Mark both reject this — *oudeni ouden eipan* is absolute, and the *gar* (for) attaches a complete explanatory clause: 'they said nothing to anyone, *because* they were afraid.' Mark is closing on a note of dread, not on a deferred announcement. Why? The likeliest critical explanation, from scholars like Crossan and Norman Petersen, is that Mark's silence-ending is theologically deliberate: the gospel breaks off mid-action, throws the burden onto the reader, and warns implicitly that even the women — the last faithful witnesses — failed at the moment of proclamation. Matthew and Luke, writing later, found that ending intolerable for catechetical purposes and rewrote it. Bart Ehrman and Bruce Metzger both treat Mark 16:8 as one of the cleanest cases of subsequent gospels editorially fixing a theologically problematic Markan ending. Steel-manning the apologist: yes, you can read *oudeni* as temporally restricted to en-route silence. But the Greek doesn't support it and the early church's manufacture of multiple alternative endings shows they read Mark's ending the same way the critics do. Take your pick.
